summary: A July 1975 survey of New-Protocol Telnet servers. It is a status snapshot that updates RFC 679.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 703 reports which ARPANET TELNET servers supported the New Protocol as of July 10, 1975. It includes a host-by-host table and a summary of the options each server implemented.

questions: what is the new telnet protocol
which hosts supported new telnet in 1975
how many telnet servers supported the new protocol in july 1975
subtitle: A July 1975 survey of which ARPANET hosts ran New-Protocol TELNET servers.

tldr.problem: The network community wanted an updated view of which server hosts had implemented New-Protocol TELNET and which options they supported.
tldr.mechanism: The author used a survey program and manual checks to record server behavior as seen by the New-Protocol User TELNET at BBNA on July 10, 1975.
tldr.outcome: Of 43 server hosts, the report lists 25 New-Protocol implementations, 16 without one and two with unknown status; the unit metadata says it updates RFC 679.

today: The unit records RFC 703's status as Unknown and says it updates RFC 679. The report is a snapshot of New-Protocol TELNET servers as of July 10, 1975.

sections.title: The Survey Results
sections.content:
Dodds says that several new server sites had joined the network and that New-Protocol implementation had progressed since the previous report. The survey lists 43 server hosts: 25 with a New-Protocol implementation, 16 with none and two new hosts whose status was unknown.

These figures describe the state observed by the New-Protocol User TELNET at BBNA as of July 10, 1975. The RFC says a survey program gathered the data at various times, with manual checks used to fill gaps.
sections.plainLanguage: More than half of the 43 listed servers had a New-Protocol implementation. The survey records what one New-Protocol user program observed on July 10, 1975.

sections.title: How the Table Describes Each Host
sections.content:
The table gives each host's number, name and status on sockets 1 and 27. It uses “Old” and “New” for protocol status, “X” when no server is present at a socket, and “?” when the host could not be reached.

The options column records incoming options as I# and outgoing options as O#. The report tabulates Transmit-Binary, Echo, Suppress-Go-Ahead and Timing-Mark option numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: For each host, the table shows whether an old or new server answers on each socket. It also lists selected options the server says it will or do support.

sections.title: How to Read the Implementation Categories
sections.content:
The summary separates New-Protocol servers into three groups: 13 hosts had Old on socket 1 and New on socket 27; eight had New on sockets 1 and 27; and four had New on socket 1 only.

The author notes that some entries marked as New-Protocol servers on socket 1 may actually respond to both Old and New user TELNETs, depending on the control sequences they receive. Servers marked with an asterisk return improper responses to some TELNET option requests.
sections.plainLanguage: The report distinguishes several ways hosts offered the new server, including hosts that kept an old server too. Some classifications are qualified because servers may respond differently to old and new clients.
